newsitem.title: USA: Fed Gov. Lindsey resigns, effective Feb. 5.
newsitem.headline: Fed Gov. Lindsey resigns, effective Feb. 5.

text.p: Federal Reserve Gov. Lawrence Lindsey announced his resignation on Friday from the seven-member board that shapes the country's monetary policy and regulates part of its banking system.

In his resignation letter to President Clinton, which was dated Thursday, Lindsey said he would not attend the Feb. 4 and 5 meeting of the Fed's policy-setting Federal Open Market Committee. He said his resignation will take effect Feb. 5.

The departure of Lindsey from the Federal Reserve Board of Governors follows that of Janet Yellen, who has been appointed chairman of the White House Council of Economic Advisers. Yellen also will not attend the February FOMC meeting.

The White House said it was in the early stages of its search to fill the two vacant seats and is unlikely to have nominees in place before the next meeting of the FOMC, where Fed policymakers determine the direction of short-term interest rates about every six weeks.

"We're very early in the process and it's hard to imagine, given where we are in the process, that we would have nominees in place in time for that meeting," White House spokesman Mike McCurry told reporters.
Gene Sperling, the newly named chairman of the White House National Economic Council, is leading the search by canvasing the academic, economic and financial communities for candidates, McCurry said.
"They are casting a very wide net," McCurry added.
In his resignation letter, Lindsey praised the Fed governors with whom he has worked since his appointment by Republican President George Bush in 1991, especially Fed Chairman Alan Greenspan.
"The country has been fortunate to have had the services of each of them," Lindsey said.

"I therefore respectfully suggest that in your search for a successor to my seat on the board, that you consider my colleagues, past and present, as ideal role models for the type of individual who will be an asset to the board," he told the president.

Lindsey, 42, will join the American Enterprise Institute, a conservative Washington think tank, where he will become a resident scholar and holder of the Arthur F. Burns Chair in Economics, the Fed said.

A staunch free-market advocate and well-respected economist, Lindsey is considered well within the mainstream of the the board, which has sought to control inflationary pressure by maintaining economic growth at a moderate pace.

Over the past year, he has joined his fellow Fed governors, including Greenspan, in opposing interest rate hikes that were advocated by some of the more inflation-wary presidents of the dozen regional Federal Reserve Banks.

He also has tended to side with those who have backed away from the notion that the so-called natural rate of unemployment -- the lowest jobless rate that could be reached without triggering inflationary pressure -- was about 6 percent. The rate has been below that level for about two and a half years, with no noticable uptick in inflation.
Lindsey headed a Fed panel that implements the Community Reinvestment Act, which requires banks to make their lending policies more diverse and inclusive of inner city populations.

A former economics professor at Harvard University, Lindsey served on the staff of the White House Council of Economic Advisers under President Ronald Reagan for three years before joining the Bush administration and then becoming a Fed governor.

Lindsey called his tenure on the Fed "one of the most personally and intellectually enriching experiences of my life" and said the monetary policy it has shaped "has made our economic performance the envy of the world."
